proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Oral History and Working Class History: A Rewarding Alliance’ (2013), Sangster uses Thompson’s The Voice of the Past (second edition, 1988; first published 1978) to explain how nineteenth-century historical professionalization marginalized oral testimony.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary reading of Sangster’s own article, printed p. 1, second main paragraph and note 1: ‘as Paul Thompson noted decades ago’ and ‘marginalize oral accounts’. The paragraph uses his account in her explanation of oral history’s disciplinary position; note 1 identifies ‘Historians and oral history’, chapter 2 of the 1988 edition. The article itself identifies volume 33 (2013); the date embedded in the download filename is not substituted for that issue date. This is a bounded, explicitly attributed conceptual resource, not a claim that Thompson originated her method or mentored her. Thompson’s cited chapter was not freshly read. Distinct from his existing contribution to the oral-history field and from Sangster’s separate relationships to E. P. Thompson.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Interview with Paul Thompson’ (recorded 2018, published 2019), Thompson invokes Eric Williams’s interpretation, identified in the editorial note with Capitalism and Slavery (1944), to challenge the benevolent account of British abolition he had learned at school.
proposed_edges.map_label: Williams against the benevolent abolition story
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Thompson’s answer to André Vargas’s question about Jamaican families, colonialism and race: the paragraph beginning ‘Also, the whole story about slavery’ credits Williams with showing that the campaign to end the slave trade ‘actually benefited Britain’. Note 13 identifies Eric Williams and Capitalism & Slavery but cites a 1994 edition; UNC Press’s description, separately reopened, establishes the original 1944 publication and distinguishes the linked 2021 edition. Note 1 dates the recorded UFRJ event to June 2018; the journal header dates publication to January–April 2019. The edge records Thompson’s explicit use of Williams in this answer, not a verified first discovery by Williams, a personal connection, or proof of Williams’s historical explanation. Capitalism and Slavery and Thompson’s Jamaican monograph were not freshly read. No date of initial uptake is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his contribution to ‘Between Social Scientists: Responses to Louise A. Tilly’ (1985), Thompson defends psychological explanation in oral and social history, arguing that social relationships and psychological states belong together despite weaknesses in existing psychohistory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Thompson’s complete individually signed response, original printed pp. 19–21, through the journal’s authorized 2019 supplemental scan; PDF pp. 17–19. Printed p. 21 was also visually checked. In his final paragraph he calls existing psychohistory ‘flat-footed’ but says it addresses ‘a fundamental dimension of human cultural experience’; social relations and psychological states are ‘intimately bound up’. He identifies family relationships, sexuality and the social shaping of personality as historical questions to which oral historians can contribute. The contribution is a defence of these questions within a mixed methodological programme, not an endorsement of every psychohistorical study or a claim to found psychohistory. Although the collective heading names four respondents, the passage ends with Paul Thompson’s signature; the following response is not attributed to him. The original issue is February 1985, not the scan’s 2018 upload or the 2019 tribute. Distinct from edge_2937’s reliability/subjectivity claim and edge_2938’s participation claim.
